points.text: In cases of suspected scaphoid fracture where the initial radiographs are negative, a supplementary MRI, or alternatively CT, should be carried out within three to five days.
It is well known that scaphoid fractures can be difficult to diagnose on initial radiographs.
MRI is recommended for diagnostics, while computed tomography (CT) has proven more reliable and accurate in the assessment of scaphoid fracture characteristics and union.
At our institution, if a scaphoid fracture is presented as a hair-thin line on some radiographs but not necessarily all, or diagnosed by MRI only, we do not proceed with CT.

On early July 2026, I fell on my outstretched hand and attended the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, Accident & Emergency department. I was X-rayed and told it was a sprain, and I was sent home. The pain did not go away. On mid August 2026, my GP sent me back for a second X-ray, which showed a scaphoid fracture. By November 2026, the fracture has not healed and I now need surgery. I have also missed my second-year exams and had to stop shifts at my part-time job because I cannot use my wrist. I would like an explanation of what went wrong, treatment or support to put things right, and compensation for what happened.

Healthcare Improvement Scotland / SIGN says: "In cases of suspected scaphoid fracture where the initial radiographs are negative, a supplementary MRI, or alternatively CT, should be carried out within three to five days." Could NHS Lothian please explain how this recommendation was considered in my care?

says.detail:
Healthcare Improvement Scotland / SIGN:
In cases of suspected scaphoid fracture where the initial radiographs are negative, a supplementary MRI, or alternatively CT, should be carried out within three to five days.
It is well known that scaphoid fractures can be difficult to diagnose on initial radiographs.
MRI is recommended for diagnostics, while computed tomography (CT) has proven more reliable and accurate in the assessment of scaphoid fracture characteristics and union.
At our institution, if a scaphoid fracture is presented as a hair-thin line on some radiographs but not necessarily all, or diagnosed by MRI only, we do not proceed with CT.
Possible gaps: Did the A&E department follow the guideline by performing a supplementary MRI or CT scan within three to five days after the initial negative radiographs? | Did the A&E department consider the possibility of a scaphoid fracture despite the difficulty in diagnosing it on initial radiographs? | Did the GP follow the guideline by considering MRI or CT as more reliable diagnostic tools for scaphoid fractures, rather than relying solely on X-rays? | Did the GP follow the guideline by not proceeding with CT, even though the fracture was diagnosed by MRI only?

points.text: In cases of suspected scaphoid fracture where the initial radiographs are negative, a supplementary MRI, or alternatively CT, should be carried out within three to five days.
It is well known that scaphoid fractures can be difficult to diagnose on initial radiographs.
MRI is recommended for diagnostics, while computed tomography (CT) has proven more reliable and accurate in the assessment of scaphoid fracture characteristics and union.
At our institution, if a scaphoid fracture is presented as a hair-thin line on some radiographs but not necessarily all, or diagnosed by MRI only, we do not proceed with CT.

draft.details:
On early July 2026, I fell on my outstretched hand and attended the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, Accident & Emergency department. I was X-rayed and told it was a sprain, and I was sent home. The pain did not go away. On mid August 2026, my GP sent me back for a second X-ray, which showed a scaphoid fracture. By November 2026, the fracture has not healed and I now need surgery. I have also missed my second-year exams and had to stop shifts at my part-time job because I cannot use my wrist. I would like an explanation of what went wrong, treatment or support to put things right, and compensation for what happened.

Healthcare Improvement Scotland / SIGN says: "In cases of suspected scaphoid fracture where the initial radiographs are negative, a supplementary MRI, or alternatively CT, should be carried out within three to five days." Could NHS Lothian please explain how this recommendation was considered in my care?
